title: Design a WhatsApp-style chat
scopeHtml:
Scope: requirements, API, estimates, connection gateways, routing and ordering, groups, presence, offline and push, E2EE.

Scope: requirements, API, estimates, connection gateways, routing and ordering, groups, presence, offline and push, E2EE.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
WhatsApp-style chat lets two people (or a group) exchange messages instantly, shows delivery state (sent, delivered, read), works with flaky phones that go offline, and keeps messages private. Others: Telegram, Signal, iMessage, Messenger. The tricky parts are millions of long-lived connections, never losing or duplicating a message, per-chat ordering, and offline delivery.

Functional requirements

  • 1:1 and group chat (up to 1,024 members for WhatsApp-like groups), text plus media.
  • Delivery receipts: sent (server has it), delivered (device has it), read.
  • Online/last seen, typing indicator.
  • Offline delivery: a message is stored until the recipient comes online; push notification when offline.
  • Multi-device sync; message history on a new device (optional).
  • End-to-end encryption (E2EE) as a design constraint.

Non-functional requirements

  • Delivery latency under 200 ms when both are online.
  • Zero message loss once the server acknowledges; no duplicates visible to the user.
  • Per-conversation ordering.
  • Hundreds of millions of concurrent connections; high availability.

Decision gravity. Choose a persistent bidirectional connection (WebSocket or custom protocol over TCP) with application-level acknowledgements. Long polling or HTTP per message would multiply latency and battery use. One-way door: the protocol (ack scheme, message ids) is baked into every client you ship, and old app versions live for years.

Everyday analogy. A post office with a permanent pneumatic tube to every house; if nobody is home, letters wait in a box until the door opens.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting offline users and push notifications.
  • Not stating the delivery guarantee (at-least-once plus dedupe).
  • Skipping group chats and multi-device, which change fan-out design.

notes.title: API
notes.html:
Mostly a streaming protocol, plus REST for the non-realtime bits.

// Client to server over the persistent connection (JSON shown for readability;
// production protocols use compact binary such as Protobuf)
{ "type":"send", "clientMsgId":"c-7f31", "chatId":"chat_551", "to":"u_9",
  "ciphertext":"<base64>", "ts":1731150000123 }

// Server ack to sender (message persisted)
{ "type":"ack", "clientMsgId":"c-7f31", "serverMsgId":"m_90017", "state":"SENT", "seq":412 }

// Server pushes to recipient
{ "type":"msg", "serverMsgId":"m_90017", "chatId":"chat_551", "from":"u_3", "seq":412, "ciphertext":"..." }

// Recipient device acks
{ "type":"delivered", "serverMsgId":"m_90017" }
{ "type":"read", "chatId":"chat_551", "uptoSeq":412 }
POST /v1/media/upload-url       -> { "uploadUrl":"https://.../presigned", "mediaId":"md_5" }
GET  /v1/chats/chat_551/messages?afterSeq=400&limit=100      // catch-up after reconnect
POST /v1/groups  { "name":"Family", "members":["u_1","u_2"] } -> 201 { "groupId":"g_8" }
GET  /v1/users/u_9/keys         -> pre-key bundle for E2EE session setup

clientMsgId is the idempotency key: a retried send maps to the same message. seq is a per-chat monotonically increasing number that gives order and makes gaps detectable. Media bytes bypass the chat servers (presigned upload; the message carries the media id and decryption key).

Industry example. WhatsApp used a modified XMPP, later a custom binary protocol over a persistent TCP connection on Erlang servers; Signal uses a WebSocket to its server for the same job.

Everyday analogy. Registered post with a tracking number: you can re-send safely and the receiver can tell if one in the sequence is missing.

Common interview traps.

  • No client-generated id (retries create duplicates).
  • Ordering by timestamp only (clocks differ).
  • Sending media through the chat connection.

notes.title: Estimates
notes.html:
Assume 500M DAU, 100M concurrent connections at peak, 40 messages sent per user per day.

Quantity Calculation Result
Messages 500M x 40 20B/day, 230k/s avg, peak 700k/s
Deliveries groups multiply; assume 1.5 recipients avg ~350k to 1M deliveries/s
Message size ~100 B text + ~100 B metadata (E2EE ciphertext adds overhead) ~200 B
Storage (if retained) 20B x 200 B 4 TB/day, ~1.5 PB/year
Connections 100M concurrent / ~500k per big server 200 servers minimum; plan ~400 for headroom
Connection memory 100M x ~10 KB state ~1 TB across the fleet
Presence updates each connect/disconnect tens of thousands/s, handled lazily
Media 10% of messages x 200 KB 400 TB/day at CDN/object storage

What this tells you. The scarce resource is concurrent connections, not request rate. WhatsApp famously ran about 1-2 million connections per Erlang server in 2012 (about 2M on a tuned box, per their public posts). Messages are small. Media dominates bytes. A key design choice: WhatsApp-style systems keep messages only until delivered (server as a mailbox), cutting storage by two orders of magnitude compared with retaining history forever.

Everyday analogy. A switchboard with 100 million phone lines but short calls.

Common interview traps.

  • Sizing by requests per second and ignoring connection counts, file descriptors, and memory per connection.
  • Storing all history on servers when the product keeps it on devices.
  • Forgetting group fan-out amplification.

notes.title: High-level design
notes.html:
Components

  • Gateway (connection) servers: hold the WebSocket/TCP connections, do TLS, heartbeat, framing; stateless apart from the live socket. Each connection is identified by (userId, deviceId).
  • Session registry: a fast map userId -> [gatewayId, deviceId, lastSeen] in Redis (or an in-house service). Updated on connect/disconnect with TTL refreshed by heartbeats.
  • Chat service: validates, assigns the per-chat seq, persists, acks the sender, routes to recipients.
  • Message store: durable per-recipient mailbox/inbox: Cassandra/ScyllaDB or HBase (WhatsApp used Mnesia/Erlang early, Facebook Messenger used HBase, Discord moved from Cassandra to ScyllaDB). Partition by chatId (or recipient inbox), cluster by seq.
  • Push notifier: sends wake-ups via APNs (Apple) and FCM (Android) when the recipient is offline.
  • Media service: presigned upload to object storage, CDN download; thumbnails.
  • Group service: membership, roles, group key management.

Online path steps

  1. A sends over its socket to Gateway 1.
  2. Chat service persists the message with seq and acks A (one grey tick).
  3. Router looks up B in the session registry, pushes via B's gateway.
  4. B's device acks delivery (two ticks); server forwards the state to A. When B opens the chat, a read receipt follows (blue ticks).

Offline path: no session entry, so the message stays in B's mailbox, a push notification is sent; when B reconnects it fetches everything after its last seq and acks.

Decision gravity. Persist before ack. The sender's single tick means "the server owns this message". That is the durability commitment; the cost is a write on the critical path (about 5 ms to a Cassandra quorum), reversible only by weakening the guarantee, which users would feel as lost messages.

Industry examples. WhatsApp: Erlang/FreeBSD, mailbox model, messages deleted from servers after delivery; Discord: Elixir gateways, Cassandra to ScyllaDB for history; Slack: WebSocket gateways plus MySQL (Vitess).

Everyday analogy. The server is the mailbox at the building entrance; delivery to the flat happens when the person is home.

Common interview traps.

  • Direct server-to-server delivery without a durable store in the middle.
  • Acking the sender before persisting.
  • One global session registry as a single point of failure.

notes.title: Deep dives
notes.html:
Connections and the gateway layer

A modern Linux server can hold 1M+ idle TCP connections if tuned: raise file descriptors (ulimit -n 2000000, fs.file-max), widen ephemeral ports on the load balancer side, use epoll/kqueue with an event loop (Netty, Erlang BEAM, Go, Elixir), and keep per-connection memory small (4 to 10 KB).

# Kernel and limits sketch for a gateway host
sysctl -w fs.file-max=3000000
sysctl -w net.core.somaxconn=65535
sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1
ulimit -n 2000000
  • Heartbeats: application ping every 30 to 60 s (mobile NATs drop idle TCP after minutes); missing 2 pings marks the connection dead and removes the registry entry. Mobile uses adaptive intervals to save battery.
  • Load balancing: L4 balancer (least connections) in front; connections are long-lived so round robin makes uneven servers; draining on deploy with gradual reconnect.
  • Reconnect storms: a deploy of 200 gateways kicks 100M clients which reconnect at once. Mitigate with client jittered exponential backoff (random 1 to 30 s), rolling deploys (a few % at a time), connection draining over minutes, and admission control at the gateway.

Decision gravity. Keep gateways thin and nearly stateless: they only terminate sockets and forward frames. This makes deploys and crashes survivable (clients reconnect and catch up from seq). Alternative: put chat logic in the gateway (fewer hops, harder to deploy). Reversible with effort.

Production incident pattern. Symptom: after a deploy, message delay of minutes and a 10x spike in CPU. Metric: new connections per second, auth service latency. Cause: reconnect storm saturating login and registry. Fix: backoff with jitter, rate-limited accepts, deploy canaries.

Everyday analogy. A hotel lobby with a front desk that connects calls but does not remember conversations.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting that mobile networks silently kill idle connections.
  • Using HTTP long polling for a billion users.
  • Deploying all gateways at once.

Routing, ordering and delivery guarantees

Routing: to find B's gateway, look up the session registry. If B is on another data centre or has several devices, route to all device sessions. Large systems shard users to "home" chat servers by consistent hashing so the chat service for B (which also owns B's inbox) is determined by hash(userId); the sender's gateway forwards to B's owning node directly.

Ordering: wall-clock timestamps are not reliable. Assign a per-chat sequence number at the chat service: a counter owned by the partition that owns the chat (single writer per chat) gives strict order. For 1:1 chats the inbox of the recipient can be ordered by arrival at the server. Clients display by seq, then local time for unsent ones.

Delivery guarantee: at-least-once + dedupe = effectively once.

  • Sender retries send with the same clientMsgId until it gets the ack.
  • Server dedupes by (chatId, clientMsgId) (a unique key in the store, or a short-lived Redis set) and returns the original serverMsgId.
  • Recipient acks delivered; the server deletes (or marks) the message in its mailbox only after the ack; unacked messages are redelivered on reconnect, and the client dedupes by serverMsgId.
-- Cassandra-style model (CQL)
CREATE TABLE messages (
  chat_id   text,
  seq       bigint,
  server_msg_id text,
  sender    text,
  ciphertext blob,
  sent_at   timestamp,
  PRIMARY KEY ((chat_id), seq)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (seq DESC);
-- Idempotency via lightweight transaction or a separate dedupe table keyed by (chat_id, client_msg_id)

Gap detection: if a client receives seq 415 after 412, it asks GET messages?afterSeq=412 to fill 413 and 414.

Decision gravity. Sequence per chat from a single writer is the choice that gives order cheaply; alternatives (Lamport/vector clocks, global sequence) cost more or serialise too much. It breaks if one chat becomes a hotspot (a huge public group) so large groups use sharded streams. Changing the ordering scheme later is a one-way door visible to users as reordered history.

Everyday analogy. Numbering each page of a letter so the reader can spot a missing page and ask for it again.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming exactly-once delivery over the network.
  • Using client timestamps for ordering.
  • Deleting from the mailbox before the recipient's ack.

Groups and fan-out

For a group of N members, one send becomes N deliveries. Two strategies:

  • Fan-out on write (per-member inbox): copy a reference of the message to each member's inbox. Fast reads, write amplification N (for N=1,024 that is 1,024 writes per message).
  • Group stream (fan-out on read): store the message once in the group's stream; each member keeps a cursor (lastReadSeq). Writes are 1, reads are N (but each member reads only when active). Works well for big groups and channels (Telegram channels, Discord, Slack).

WhatsApp-sized groups (up to 1,024) use fan-out on write with small payloads; big communities use the stream model. Group E2EE uses sender keys: each member distributes a sender key to others once, and each message is encrypted once with the sender's key, so the server stores one ciphertext rather than N.

Membership changes (removing someone) need key rotation so they cannot read future messages.

Decision gravity. Group size limits are product decisions that quietly protect the architecture (a 1,024 cap keeps fan-out bounded). Raising limits later forces the stream model, a heavy migration.

Industry example. WhatsApp group limit moved from 256 to 512 to 1,024 members; Discord and Telegram use stream/channel models with millions of members.

Everyday analogy. A noticeboard in the club (stream) versus a photocopy placed in every member's pigeonhole (inbox).

Common interview traps.

  • Treating a 100k-member group as 100k inbox writes per message.
  • Forgetting key rotation on member removal.

Presence, typing and receipts

Presence (online, last seen) is high-churn data; do not persist every change. Keep lastSeen in the registry (updated with heartbeats, flushed to a DB every few minutes). A user's contacts subscribe to their presence only when the chat is open; broadcasting presence to 500 contacts for every flap would multiply load. Debounce flaps (do not announce offline for 10 s after disconnect) and send typing events through the existing connection with a 3 s expiry and no persistence.

Read receipts are batched: send read upto seq, not one per message. Privacy setting to hide last seen/read receipts is checked on the server before sending.

Common interview traps.

  • Persisting each typing event.
  • Fan-out of presence to all contacts.
  • Per-message read receipts instead of a cursor.

Offline delivery, push and multi-device

When B is offline: message waits in B's mailbox (TTL 30 days in WhatsApp-like systems, then dropped). The push notifier sends a generic wake-up through APNs/FCM (with E2EE the push often carries no content, only "you have a message", so the phone wakes the app which fetches and decrypts). Push is unreliable (throttled, collapsed), so it is a hint; the source of truth is the mailbox fetched on connect.

Multi-device: each device has its own identity key, session and mailbox cursor. The sender encrypts per recipient device (Signal protocol fan-out), or a linked device syncs history from the primary (WhatsApp's earlier model) / server-assisted encrypted backup (newer). Server routes to all active devices; receipts from any device count as delivered.

Decision gravity. Treating push as a hint and the mailbox as truth means you can lose pushes without losing messages. The per-device encryption sessions are a significant complexity cost to accept for E2EE; it is a one-way door for the product's privacy promise.

Everyday analogy. The doorbell tells you there is a parcel; the parcel is in the locker whether you hear the bell or not.

Common interview traps.

  • Relying on push notifications to carry the message.
  • Single-device mental model for multi-device.
  • Putting message text in push payloads for an E2EE product.

End-to-end encryption in one page

The server must not read messages. Signal protocol (used by WhatsApp, Signal, Messenger secret chats): each user publishes a pre-key bundle (identity key, signed pre-key, one-time pre-keys) to the server. To start a chat, A fetches B's bundle, runs X3DH to derive a shared secret, then uses the Double Ratchet to derive a fresh key per message (forward secrecy and post-compromise security). Server stores only ciphertext and routing metadata.

Consequences: the server cannot do server-side search or spam scanning on content (use client-side reports, metadata signals), backups need separate encryption (user passphrase or key), and key changes trigger "security code changed" warnings.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "we encrypt with TLS" and calling it E2EE.
  • Forgetting that E2EE removes server-side features.

notes.title: What interviewers look for
notes.html:
• Connection layer thinking: persistent connections, heartbeats, tuned servers, reconnect storms.
  • Numbers: 100M concurrent connections, 700k msgs/s, storage as a mailbox vs full history.
  • Delivery semantics: persist before ack, client ids, per-chat seq, dedupe, receipt ladder.
  • Offline and push handled correctly with the mailbox as truth.
  • Group fan-out trade-offs and E2EE consequences.
  • Failure thinking: gateway crash, registry stale entry, DC outage, duplicate delivery.
  • Seniors discuss multi-region, key management, abuse prevention without reading content, and cost of media.

Common interview traps.

  • Hand-waving the connection scale.
  • Ignoring ordering within a chat.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Chat is a connection-scale problem: 100M concurrent sockets across hundreds of gateway servers with heartbeats and jittered reconnects.
  • Persist then ack; at-least-once delivery plus client ids and per-chat seq gives ordered, deduplicated, effectively once delivery.
  • Session registry maps users to gateways; the message store is a per-chat or per-user mailbox in a wide-column DB.
  • Groups: inbox fan-out for small groups, shared stream with cursors for large ones.
  • Offline: mailbox is the truth, push is only a wake-up; presence and typing are ephemeral.
  • E2EE (Signal protocol) keeps servers blind to content and shapes backups, search and multi-device design.

questions.subtopic: Persist before ack and the tick ladder
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through what the single tick, double tick and blue tick mean in the server, and why the server must persist before acknowledging the sender.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests delivery semantics: who owns the message at each moment.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: One tick means the server persisted the message and now owns it. Two ticks mean the recipient's device acked delivery. Blue ticks mean the recipient read it. I persist before acking because the ack is a durability promise: if I ack and then crash before writing, the sender believes it is safe and the message is gone.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Sender -> Gateway -> Chat service: assign seq, persist -> ack SENT
Chat service -> registry lookup -> Recipient gateway -> device -> ack DELIVERED -> forward to sender
Recipient opens chat -> read upto seq -> READ

Persist costs about 5 ms on a quorum write to a wide-column store; that is the price of the promise. If the recipient is offline the message stays in the mailbox and a push wakes the device. Receipts are batched: read upto seq, not per message.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Acking before persistence.
  • Deleting from the mailbox before the recipient ack.
  • Direct server-to-server delivery with no durable store.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Sender retries after a lost ack? -> Same clientMsgId; server dedupes and returns the original id.
  2. Ordering? -> Per-chat seq from a single writer, not timestamps.
  3. When may the server delete? -> After the recipient's delivered ack (mailbox model).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: lists the ticks. Senior: ties each state to a durability or ownership boundary and names the cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A chat team that acked from memory and wrote asynchronously lost messages on node crashes and had no way to detect it.

questions.promptHtml: How do you deliver one message to a 1,000-member group versus a 1,000,000-member channel?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests write amplification reasoning and knowing when to switch models.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: For up to about a thousand members I fan out on write: copy a reference into each member's inbox, 1,024 small writes, fast reads. For huge channels I store the message once in the group stream and each member keeps a cursor (lastReadSeq); writes are one, reads happen only for active members. Group E2EE uses sender keys so the server stores one ciphertext, not N.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Small group: Sender -> Chat service -> inbox of member 1..N (N writes) -> online: push, offline: push notification
Large channel: Sender -> Chat service -> group stream (1 write); members pull from cursor

A group size cap is a product decision that protects the architecture. Raising it later forces the stream model, a heavy migration. Membership changes require key rotation so removed members cannot read future messages.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• 100k inbox writes per message.
  • Forgetting key rotation on removal.
  • Notifying all members' devices when most are muted.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Read receipts in a huge group? -> Aggregate counts, not per member.
  2. Ordering in a hot group? -> One writer per stream; shard the stream for extreme sizes.
  3. Presence in groups? -> Not broadcast; subscribe on open.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "write to all members". Senior: two models with thresholds, E2EE sender keys, and the cap as an architectural lever.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Raising the group size cap from 256 to thousands without changing fan-out saturated writers on big-group messages.

questions.contextHtml: Launch in a new market: 20M DAU, peak 6M concurrent connections, 30 messages per user per day, average 1.4 recipients per message. Proposed gateway servers: 16 cores, 64 GB RAM, tuned to 400k connections each. A manager says "20M DAU is about 7,000 requests per second, we need 4 servers".
questions.promptHtml: Size the gateway fleet and the message path, and correct the manager.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Sizes by request rate only; forgets memory, file descriptors and headroom.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Peak-to-average ratio? Media share? Retention of history on server? Number of regions?
  2. Immediate mitigation: n/a.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The scarce resource is concurrent connections, then memory per connection, then message throughput.
  4. How I'd verify each: The math:
Messages   20M x 30 = 600M/day = ~7k/s avg, peak ~3x = ~21k/s ; deliveries x1.4 = ~30k/s
Gateways   6M / 400k = 15 servers minimum ; N+2 and 60% target utilisation => ~25 to 30
Memory     6M x 10 KB = 60 GB total state (about 2 to 4 GB per server) - fine
FDs        ulimit -n above 500k, fs.file-max raised
Storage    mailbox model: only undelivered messages; 600M x 200 B = 120 GB/day if retained
  1. Root cause: The manager's request rate is right (about 7k/s) but the constraint is sockets: 6M idle connections need servers regardless of message rate.
  2. Fix: About 30 gateways across 2 or 3 zones, so losing one zone leaves enough capacity; plan reconnect: a zone loss pushes 2M clients to reconnect, so keep headroom and jittered backoff. Chat service and registry sized separately by message rate.
  3. Prevention: Track connections per server, fd usage, heartbeats, reconnect rate.
  4. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not run at 100% of the tested connection density; failure of one zone must be absorbed.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Growth 5x? -> Roughly 5x gateways and registry shards; messages still modest.
  • Media? -> Bypasses gateways: presigned upload and CDN.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Capacity was sized for steady state; a regional network blip dropped 1.5M connections and the fleet could not accept the reconnect burst.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: size by RPS.
  • Hire: sockets drive fleet size.
  • Strong hire: zone-loss headroom, fd and memory, mailbox storage reasoning.

questions.contextHtml:
On poor networks users see the same message twice and the sender sees it sent twice. Server log excerpt:

10:01:02.100 recv send chatId=551 clientMsgId=<none> from=u_3 ts=1731150062100
10:01:02.130 persist seq=412 server_msg_id=m_90017
10:01:02.131 ack-write FAILED connection reset
10:01:07.400 recv send chatId=551 clientMsgId=<none> from=u_3 ts=1731150067400
10:01:07.431 persist seq=413 server_msg_id=m_90018

The client retries a send if no ack arrives within 5 s. The send frame has no client-generated id.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the bug and the fix, including the receiver side.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Dedupes by message text and timestamp, which merges legitimate repeated "ok" messages.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are old app versions still in the field? Where does the client store unsent messages?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-side best effort dedupe is unsafe; ship the client fix, then support old versions with a server compatibility path.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Ack lost after persist plus retry without an idempotency key; recipient re-delivery after missing the delivered ack.
  4. How I'd verify each: Look for pairs of messages with same sender and body within the retry window.
  5. Root cause: At-least-once retry without an idempotency key creates a new message each time.
  6. Fix: Client generates clientMsgId (UUID) per logical send and reuses it on retries; server has a unique (chat_id, client_msg_id) key (lightweight transaction, or a dedupe table/short-lived Redis set) and returns the original serverMsgId and seq. Receiver dedupes by serverMsgId and uses seq to detect gaps.
  7. Prevention: Fault injection tests dropping acks; metric for dedupe hits.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The id is a protocol field baked into every client for years (one-way door). I would not rely on exactly-once delivery over the network.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Dedupe window? -> At least as long as client retry plus offline queue time; store with TTL days.
  • Dedupe store loses data? -> Fall back to the unique key in the message table.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A release without a client id doubled every message during a carrier outage; the fix needed a forced upgrade.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: dedupe by content.
  • Hire: clientMsgId with unique key.
  • Strong hire: receiver dedupe, window sizing, old-client compatibility.

questions.contextHtml: Users report conversations showing replies before questions, but only for people on two different phones. The client sorts messages by the sender's local ts. One sender's phone clock is 3 minutes fast. Also, after a flaky reconnect a recipient shows seq 410, 411, 415 with 412 to 414 missing until app restart.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Sync clocks with NTP" or use server timestamps only.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who assigns sequence numbers today? One writer per chat? Do clients fetch after reconnect?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Client sorts by server seq, shows unsent messages by local time at the bottom.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Client-time ordering (clock skew), no gap detection after reconnect, possible multiple writers per chat.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare device clocks, log seq receipt order on reconnect.
  5. Root cause: Wall clocks differ across devices; the client never asks for missing seqs.
  6. Fix: Single writer per chat assigns monotonically increasing seq at the owning partition; the client displays by seq. On receiving seq 415 after 412 it calls GET /chats/551/messages?afterSeq=412 to fill gaps; on reconnect it always catches up from its last acked seq.
Cassandra-style: PRIMARY KEY ((chat_id), seq) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (seq DESC)
  1. Prevention: Test: kill the connection mid-delivery and assert no gaps.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Single writer per chat gives cheap strict order but a hot group becomes a hotspot (shard large streams); a global sequence serialises everything; vector clocks are heavier. Changing the scheme later is visible as reordered history.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Multi-device sender? -> Seq is per chat on the server, so all devices agree.
  • Writer node fails over? -> New owner continues from the highest persisted seq.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A phone with a wrong clock made every chat with it look inverted for a week until sorting moved to server seq.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: clocks.
  • Hire: server seq plus gap fill.
  • Strong hire: single-writer reasoning, hotspot limits, failover continuity.

questions.contextHtml: A rolling deploy of 200 gateways restarts them 20 at a time every 2 minutes with 90 s draining. After the third batch, auth latency goes from 20 ms to 4 s, Redis session registry CPU at 98%, delivery delay "minutes", gateway accept queue overflowing (netstat -s: 1.2M SYNs to LISTEN sockets dropped). Clients reconnect immediately on disconnect with a fixed 1 s retry. 100M clients are connected; each batch drops about 10M.
questions.promptHtml: What is happening, and what do you change in the client, the deploy and the server?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Scales up auth only.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is there accept rate limiting? How heavy is the connect path (auth, registry write, catch-up fetch)? Can we pause the deploy?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause the deploy, enable admission control (accept at a capped rate and reject with a retry-after), temporarily relax expensive connect work (defer catch-up fetch).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Fixed-interval reconnects creating synchronized waves, connect path too heavy per client, batch too large, registry write amplification.
  4. How I'd verify each: New connections per second, auth QPS, registry ops per second, SYN drops.
  5. Root cause: 10M clients per batch reconnect at once with no jitter; each connect does TLS, auth, registry write and catch-up.
  6. Fix: Client exponential backoff with full jitter (1 to 30 s), server-sent backoff hints, rolling deploys at a few percent at a time with canary, drain connections over minutes by gradually closing, rate-limited accepts, light resume tokens instead of full auth, registry entries with TTL refreshed by heartbeat so no mass deletes.
  7. Prevention: Deploy tooling that watches connect rate and halts automatically; load test a 10M reconnect.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Slower deploys and some users offline longer; far better than a cascading outage. I would not deploy all gateways at once, and I would not size auth for the worst-case burst instead of shaping it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Old clients ignore backoff hints? -> Gateway-side accept shaping protects the core.
  • Push wakeups during the storm? -> Mailbox remains truth; the delay is catch-up, not loss.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A well-meaning one-second retry loop turned a 2-minute gateway restart into a 40-minute brownout until jitter shipped.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scale auth.
  • Hire: backoff with jitter, smaller batches.
  • Strong hire: admission control, draining, resume tokens, automated deploy halts.

questions.contextHtml: A gateway host crashes at 14:00. Over the next minutes the support desk sees: senders show two ticks (delivered) but recipients never received messages; some messages show one tick forever. The registry still maps 400k users to the dead gateway for 90 s TTL (heartbeat TTL 90 s). Router logs: push to gw-77 timed out repeated. Redis registry is healthy.
questions.promptHtml: Explain how messages were mis-acknowledged or stuck, and fix the delivery path.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Lowers the TTL to 1 s, which flaps live users.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who sets "delivered": the router or the device ack? Do messages stay in the mailbox until the device ack?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remove entries for the dead gateway by gateway id and have clients reconnect elsewhere; re-queue messages whose delivery was not acked.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Delivered state set on router send instead of device ack; mailbox cleared on send; stale registry window; no retry after a gateway timeout.
  4. How I'd verify each: Trace a message id through persist, route, gateway write and device ack timestamps.
  5. Root cause: Delivery was marked at hand-off to the gateway rather than on the device ack, and unacked messages were not redelivered; the stale registry hides the problem for up to 90 s.
  6. Fix: State machine: SENT on persist, DELIVERED only on device delivered ack; keep messages in the mailbox until acked; router treats a timeout as "not delivered", retries and falls back to push; recipients catch up with afterSeq on reconnect; registry entries tied to gateway epoch so a dead gateway invalidates all its entries at once (health-checker publishes the failure).
  7. Prevention: Chaos test killing a gateway under load; alert on messages unacked longer than 30 s.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Slightly more mailbox storage and some duplicate redelivery (client dedupe by serverMsgId) in exchange for no loss. I would not set TTL near the heartbeat interval.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Registry is a single point of failure? -> Shard it by user, replicate; clients fall back to catch-up if lookup fails.
  • Multi-device? -> Delivered when any device acks; others catch up from their own cursors.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A crash showed double ticks for messages that were never delivered, which looked like data loss to users because trust in ticks was misplaced.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: shorten TTL.
  • Hire: ack on device, keep in mailbox.
  • Strong hire: epoch invalidation, retry and push fallback, chaos testing.

questions.contextHtml: Product wants three things for the E2EE chat: server-side message search for users, automatic spam and scam scanning, and keeping history on a new phone. Security says E2EE is a non-negotiable promise. The server today stores ciphertext and routing metadata only. Backups are plaintext in cloud storage "for now".
questions.promptHtml: What do you recommend for each request, and what do you refuse?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds server-side decryption for convenience, or says "TLS is enough" for E2EE.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is E2EE a marketing promise or a regulatory need? Who needs search: users on their own history only? Abuse volume today?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Close the plaintext backup gap first; it silently breaks the promise.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Each feature that needs plaintext on the server contradicts E2EE; each has a client-side or metadata alternative.
  4. How I'd verify each: Threat-model review per feature; check what the server can see today.
  5. Root cause: n/a; the constraint shapes the design.
  6. Fix (recommendations): Search: build an on-device index (SQLite FTS) on each client. Spam: use metadata signals (rate limits, account age, report counts), client-side hash lists and user reports with the reporter forwarding the message plaintext voluntarily. History on a new phone: encrypted backup with a user-held key or passphrase, or device-to-device transfer through the Signal-style linked-device flow; per-device keys and per-device encryption fan-out.
  7. Prevention: Written privacy invariants ("server never sees plaintext") tested in design review.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add server-side decryption or key escrow without an explicit product and legal decision; it is a one-way door for user trust. Cost: weaker abuse detection and heavier clients.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Member removed from group? -> Rotate sender keys.
  • Key change on a contact? -> "Security code changed" warning, never silent.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team added server-side scanning "temporarily" and a regulator later asked why plaintext existed on servers; the on-device approach would have avoided the question.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: breaks E2EE or claims TLS suffices.
  • Hire: client-side search and metadata abuse signals.
  • Strong hire: backup key design, multi-device sessions, key rotation, explicit one-way door framing.
